title: Variance and Assignability
learning_outcomes: Explain covariance and contravariance in the context of variance and assignability.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn variance and assignability through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Model the narrowest honest type contract. Prefer inference where it is clear, use unknown at untrusted boundaries, and use control-flow checks before performing operations that depend on a value’s shape.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Variance and Assignability.** This lesson belongs to **Generics and Reusable Components**. Start by identifying the problem that variance and assignability solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Covariance and contravariance
items.text: For covariance and contravariance, preserve the relationship between input types and output types, then check representative positive and negative cases. Prefer a readable type transformation over a clever but difficult-to-maintain abstraction.

items.title: Function parameter compatibility
items.text: For function parameter compatibility, write down the input contract and the result contract. Let TypeScript infer obvious local types, and add annotations where they clarify a public API, callback, or boundary.

items.title: Variance annotations and their limitations
items.text: For variance annotations and their limitations, preserve the relationship between input types and output types, then check representative positive and negative cases. Prefer a readable type transformation over a clever but difficult-to-maintain abstraction.

content_blocks.title: Example: Variance and Assignability
content_blocks.expected_output: Producer produces T and Consumer accepts T. Variance annotations have limited use; ordinary inference and assignability remain the main tools.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Variance and Assignability”. Demonstrate covariance and contravariance, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Covariance and contravariance” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Variance and Assignability is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Covariance and contravariance, Function parameter compatibility, Variance annotations and their limitations.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
